proposal: The chapter recommends that Treasury work with Congress to replace the current individual income tax with two rates (15 percent and 30 percent), remove most deductions, credits and exclusions, cut the corporate rate to 18 percent, tax capital gains and qualified dividends at 15 percent, and allow immediate expensing. Over the longer term it favors a consumption-based tax (a national sales tax, business transfer tax, flat tax or cash-flow tax) and a three-fifths vote requirement to raise income or corporate rates.

status_summary: Public Law 119-21, signed 2025-07-04, made the 2017 individual rate schedules permanent rather than adopting a two-rate system: the U.S. Code reproduction of 26 U.S.C. 1 shows that section 70101 struck the January 1, 2026 end date from subsection (j), which keeps seven rates from 10 to 37 percent, and the IRS 2026 inflation-adjustment release of 2025-10-09 lists the same seven rates. The 21 percent corporate rate set in 2017 was left in place (the Code page for 26 U.S.C. 11 states 21 percent and lists no 2025 amendment, and the enrolled law's table of contents has no section on the corporate rate), while the law made 100 percent expensing of qualifying property permanent according to a law-firm summary, which overlaps with the chapter's expensing recommendation. A later reconciliation law, Public Law 119-98 (S. 2, Secure America Act, approved 2026-06-10), lists only homeland security appropriations sections in its table of contents and has no rate provision. No Treasury, White House or congressional proposal for the 15/30 structure, the 18 percent corporate rate, a consumption tax or a three-fifths vote requirement was found through October 2026.

timeline.event: Public Law 119-21 (H.R. 1) enacted. Per the U.S. Code reproduction of 26 U.S.C. 1, its section 70101 struck the January 1, 2026 end date from subsection (j), whose rate tables keep seven individual rates (10, 12, 22, 24, 32, 35 and 37 percent); the amendment notes cite 139 Stat. 158.

timeline.event: A law-firm summary reports that the 2017 income tax brackets were made permanent with a 37 percent top rate and that 100 percent bonus depreciation was made permanent (publication month August 2025; day set to the first of the month).

IRS release IR-2025-103 on tax year 2026 inflation adjustments lists seven individual rates (10, 12, 22, 24, 32, 35 and 37 percent), a 37 percent top rate, and a $32,200 standard deduction for joint filers.

Public Law 119-98 (S. 2, Secure America Act), a reconciliation law under title II of S. Con. Res. 33, is approved. Its table of contents lists only homeland security appropriations sections (Title I, Sections 101 to 104; Title II, Sections 201 to 203) and no individual or corporate tax rate provision.

uncertainties: The unchanged 21 percent corporate rate rests on the law.cornell.edu copy of 26 U.S.C. 11, the law's table of contents and summaries that list no change; the operative text of Title VII was not read on govinfo.gov. The IRS release lists seven rates but does not itself say the rates were made permanent. Two searches for 2026 tax proposals (a second reconciliation package, a corporate rate cut, a flat tax) returned only 2025-era material, so the absence of a 2026 proposal for the 15/30 structure is a no-result finding, not a confirmation; Congress.gov could not be read. The choice of diverged over not_started is a judgment call. Update 2026-10-15: searches for a second reconciliation tax bill and the 2027 inflation adjustments found no enacted or advancing change to rate structure; a CBS News piece of 2026-09-11 reports Bloomberg Tax projections only (the IRS 2027 release had not appeared), with seven brackets, so the structure is unchanged. A no-result finding, not confirmation. A further search on 2026-10-15 for an IRS 2027 inflation-adjustment release found only projections (no IRS release yet). Update 2026-10-16: the IRS inflation-adjusted items page (last updated 2025-12-01) lists tax year 2026 as the latest year and no tax year 2027 release; a Federal Register query for corporate tax rate documents since 2025-10-10 returned only a Treasury and IRS proposed rule on a section 250 matter (2026-08-20), which does not change rates; searches for a second reconciliation bill returned only 2025-era material. These are no-result findings, not confirmation. Update 2026-10-22: the law.cornell.edu copy of 26 U.S.C. 1 was read; its notes cite section 70101(a) and (b) of the 2025 law (2025-07-04, 139 Stat. 158), show subsection (j) headed for taxable years beginning after 2017 with the January 1, 2026 end date struck, and list the seven rates in the subsection (j)(2) tables. The notes also record a section 70101(b) change to the inflation-adjustment rule in subsection (j)(3)(B)(i), whose text was not examined. The same host's copy of 26 U.S.C. 11 states 21 percent and its latest listed amendment is from 2022; because the host's page for section 1 does reflect the 2025 law, the missing 2025 note on section 11 is read as no amendment, an inference from absence. The enacted-law PDF on govinfo.gov ends partway through its first title (section 10507) when opened, so the body of section 70101 and its effective-date clause were not read there; an external retrieval reports applicability to taxable years beginning after 2025-12-31 and no two-rate structure or 18 percent rate anywhere in the law, which was not independently reproduced. The table of contents of Public Law 119-98 (S. 2, Secure America Act, approved 2026-06-10, a reconciliation law under title II of S. Con. Res. 33) was opened on govinfo.gov: its two titles (Sections 101 to 104 and Sections 201 to 203) cover homeland security appropriations and contain no individual or corporate rate provision; the operative section text was not read. An external retrieval ran 15 searches on 2026-10-22 (web and Congress.gov) and reported no 2026 federal bill proposing a two-rate individual income tax or an 18 percent corporate rate; those searches cannot be reproduced here and are not an exhaustive full-text search of 2026 bills. It reported that results for a two-rate structure were a state law and results for an 18 percent corporate rate were a 2021 House proposal, and that the FairTax Act (H.R. 25) proposes a national retail sales tax in place of income taxes, which is related context for the chapter's long-term consumption-tax idea but not a two-rate income tax and not a match. It also described a January 2026 framework from the Republican Study Committee for a second reconciliation bill as covering housing, health care, energy, home savings and workforce items only; that framework was not opened. These remain no-result findings, not confirmation.
